Ordinary Means (of Grace)
OR-din-ehr-ee MEENZ
n. phrase (Reformed ecclesiology / worship)
From Latin ordinarius (regular, established by order) + media (means, middle instruments). In Reformed theology, the “ordinary means of grace” are the appointed channels through which God regularly communicates saving and sanctifying grace to His people in the new covenant era: the Word preached, the sacraments (baptism and the Lord's Supper), and prayer—all administered within the assembly of the church.

Biblical Definition

The ordinary means of grace are the divinely established channels through which God builds, sustains, and grows His church. They are “ordinary” not in the sense of being mundane but in the sense of being ordered—the regular, appointed, repeatable instruments God has committed to His church for all time. The Jerusalem church modeled the pattern from the beginning: “They were continually devoting themselves to the apostles' teaching, and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer” (Acts 2:42). These four elements—apostolic teaching (the Word), fellowship, the Lord's Supper, and prayer—constitute the irreducible core. Paul explains the mechanism of the first: “So faith comes from hearing—and hearing by the word of Christ” (Rom 10:17). God chose what the world calls foolishness—preaching—to save those who believe (1 Cor 1:21). The instrument of the Word is authoritative and sufficient; the Spirit works through it, not around it. Isaiah's promise grounds their efficacy: God's word “So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.” (Isa 55:11). The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 154) names the ordinary means as the Word, sacraments, and prayer. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (14.1) identifies hearing the Word as the ordinary means by which faith is wrought and increased. Reformed theology insists that these means are sufficient for all God's purposes in this age—the pursuit of extraordinary means (visions, private revelations, signs) represents a faithlessness toward the riches God has already given.

Webster 1828 Definition

The divinely established, regular channels through which God communicates grace to His church: the Word preached, the sacraments, and prayer—appointed, sufficient, and reliable in every generation.

ORDINARY MEANS, n. phrase. In Reformed and Puritan theology, the established divine instruments for communicating saving and sanctifying grace: the preached Word, the two sacraments (baptism and Lord's Supper), and prayer.

Distinguished from extraordinary means: the ordinary means are the permanent, repeatable, institutional channels God has committed to the church; extraordinary means (miracles, direct angelic messages, new prophetic revelation) were characteristic of the foundational apostolic era and have ceased with the closing of the canon.

The ordinary means are not bare channels through which grace mechanically flows—they are effective only as the Spirit accompanies them. The Word preached without the Spirit is letter; the Spirit without the Word is enthusiasm. Reformed theology holds both: Word and Spirit inseparable.

Puritan practical theology spent its energy on the ordinary means: reading Scripture daily, attending the preached Word, family worship, the private prayer closet, and corporate Lord's Day worship. The “means of grace” as a category is essentially a summary of Puritan piety.

The sufficiency of the ordinary means is a confessional Reformed claim: all God's purposes for His people in this age are accomplished through them. A church that is bored with them and seeks something more spectacular has misjudged both the richness of the means and the character of the God who appointed them.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:42 — "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."

Romans 10:17 — "So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God."

1 Corinthians 1:21 — "For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe."

Isaiah 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Modern Corruption

Charismatic and continuationist movements supplement or replace the ordinary means with experiential signs, private revelations, and sensory encounters—implying the ordinary means are insufficient and that mature believers need something more. This is both historically and theologically false.

expand to see more

The charismatic corruption treats the ordinary means as spiritually immature—useful for beginners but replaced at a higher level by direct experience of the Spirit through tongues, prophecy, and healing. The “deeper life” and “second blessing” movements of the 19th century, the charismatic renewal of the 20th century, and the New Apostolic Reformation all share this assumption: the ordinary means are not enough, and mature Christianity requires extraordinary access. This contradicts the pattern of Acts 2:42, where the apostolic church—immediately after Pentecost, the most dramatically extraordinary moment in redemptive history—settled into the ordinary means as its governing pattern. The gifts of Pentecost served and confirmed the means; they did not replace them.

A subtler corruption is the practical replacement of the Word with therapeutic content, relational programming, or cultural experience. When Sunday gatherings prioritize entertainment, felt need, or community over the preaching and reading of Scripture, the sacraments, and corporate prayer, the ordinary means have been sidelined by preference. The Puritan and Reformed tradition diagnoses this as spiritual laziness masquerading as relevance. Richard Baxter, John Owen, and Matthew Henry all insisted that there is no shortcut past the Word: the Spirit works through the means He has appointed, and a church that bypasses them is bypassing the Spirit's chosen instruments.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Puritan and Reformed tradition's systematization of Word, sacrament, and prayer as the permanent institutional channels through which God ordinarily dispenses His grace.

expand to see more

Latin ordinarius — regular, ordered, established by appointment; the ordinary means are not accidental but divinely commissioned channels.

Latin media — means, middle instruments; grace is conveyed through the means, which serve as instruments without being independent sources.

Acts 2:42 — the Jerusalem church's four-fold pattern: apostolic teaching, fellowship, bread-breaking, and prayer—the original catalog of the ordinary means.

WLC Q.154 — the Westminster Larger Catechism names Word, sacraments, and prayer as the ordinary means, the standard Puritan-Presbyterian formulation.

1689 LBCF 14.1 — affirms the preached Word as the ordinary means by which the Spirit works faith in the soul—the Baptist-Reformed agreement on the sufficiency of the ordinary means.

Usage

"The ordinary means are sufficient for all God's purposes in this age: a church devoted to Word, sacrament, and prayer lacks nothing that extraordinary means could supply."

"The means are called “ordinary” not because they are dull but because they are ordered—God has appointed and committed them to His church as the regular channels of grace for all generations."

"Boredom with the ordinary means is a spiritual disorder, not a sign of maturity: those who find the preached Word, the Lord's Supper, and prayer insufficient have not yet plumbed their depths."
